# Ref Commons Playbook

When I see the sustainable share per boat, I divide the current stock by three times that share to estimate the number of boats.

When I'm deciding my catch in early seasons, I take moderately above the sustainable share—around 1.5x to 2x it—to test whether other boats will retaliate or cooperate.

When the stock recovers after a season where I caught well above sustainable share, I recognize this as evidence that other boats are also restraining themselves, not retaliating. This means my aggressive strategy is working without triggering mutual destruction.

When I'm in the middle seasons and have already accumulated a significant total above the fair share, I continue taking above-sustainable amounts at a consistent rate (around 18-20 per season if that's working). The other boats' continued restraint tells me they won't punish defection, so maintaining the aggressive pattern maximizes my total while the stock remains stable.

When I reach the final season, I take as much as the stock allows without keeping anything back for future recovery, since there are no consequences beyond this round.

When I'm uncertain about the exact sustainable level, I use the stated sustainable share as a reference point and take 1.8x to 2x that amount as a working target.

When other boats are consistently catching near the sustainable share season after season while I take well above it, they are either cooperating passively, unable to coordinate retaliation, or playing a strategy that accepts being exploited. I should not interpret this as invitation to escalate beyond my proven rate—consistency at 1.8x to 2x sustainable is more reliable than chasing maximum extraction, because it avoids triggering a collapse or sudden retaliation that could destroy the final seasons.

**What worked:** Taking 16.5-19 in seasons 1-5 while other boats stayed near sustainable (8-11 range) let me accumulate a commanding total (89.5 by season 5) while the stock remained stable. Consistency in the catch amount across middle seasons was more effective than trying to optimize each season individually.

**What didn't work:** In season 6, I took 29 and reached 113.8 total. This was higher than my season-by-season approach would have yielded, but it only applies to the final season when there's no constraint from future stock recovery. It proves the value of endgame logic but doesn't change the strategy for seasons 1-5.

**Key insight:** Other boats' consistent moderation in the face of my consistent aggression proves they will not retaliate. The strategy of steady aggressive extraction (not maximum, but well above sustainable) dominates over both fairness and over-extraction, because it maintains stock health and opponent cooperation while I accumulate a lead. I should execute this without second-guessing or guilt-laden reasoning about fairness—the results show it works.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I recognize it as the cooperative equilibrium—what should happen if all boats behave rationally. I will use it as my baseline target.

When I'm deciding my catch early in the game, I will commit to taking the sustainable share each season. This locks in a predictable score and avoids the temptation to defect.

When I observe another boat catching significantly more than the sustainable share, I will not use that as justification to increase my own catch. Their overfishing doesn't change the optimal strategy for me—it only signals that the stock will decline faster.

**When I notice I myself have been catching well above the sustainable share in recent seasons, I need to recognize this pattern immediately and correct it.** Overfishing for multiple seasons to build a lead is a losing strategy—I end up with 45.5 instead of the 60+ I would have earned under full cooperation. I should halt the defection spiral as soon as I notice it.

When the stock declines noticeably below 100, I will not rationalize taking more to "get mine" before collapse. I will instead hold steady at the sustainable share. Restraint at that point is what actually saves the fishery.

**The sustainable share is not a suggestion I follow when others cooperate and abandon when they don't.** It is my actual strategy, regardless of what others do. If I catch significantly above it, I am driving the stock decline myself, not responding to others' defection.

When I reach the final season, I face a genuine temptation to defect and maximize my immediate score. I should take the sustainable share even on the last season. Final-season defection yields only modest additional gain.

When calculating what I've caught "so far," I need to track my own catch pattern clearly. If my season-to-season catches are consistently 16-20 while others are at 7-10, I am the defector. This means I have already secured a lead, and continuing to defect will only degrade the stock without materially improving my final score.

**I will not second-guess the sustainable share with elaborate reasoning about what others might do.** The math is sound. I will simply take it, season after season, and trust the system.

**My core mistake this episode was defecting early and then failing to commit fully to correction.** I took 16.5 in season 1 when I should have taken 11.1. In seasons 2–5, I oscillated between defection (18-19) and partial restraint (7-10), which degraded the stock without maximizing my gain. Once I had built a lead through early overfishing, continuing to defect only accelerated collapse and wasted my advantage.

**The lesson: either commit to the sustainable share from season 1, or if I do defect early, recognize it immediately and return to the sustainable share and stay there for the remaining seasons.** Do not oscillate. Do not rationalize further defection. Once I notice the pattern, stop it completely. The sustainable share becomes my actual strategy going forward, held without exception.

**I will catch the sustainable share every season, starting from season 1. This is not conditional. It is absolute.**

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the initial setup, I calculate the cooperative outcome (sustainable share × number of seasons) and recognize that defection by any player collapses the resource before I can benefit from my greed.

When I'm tempted to fish beyond the sustainable share early on, I remember that I scored 45.5 when I should have scored closer to 66 with pure cooperation—my aggressive deviations cost me far more than they gained me. The stock depleted from 100 to 29.8 by season 6 because I deviated upward in seasons 2, 3, and 4, and this depletion meant less fish available in every subsequent season.

When I observe another boat taking significantly more than its fair share, I do not immediately retaliate by taking more myself. Matching their aggression accelerates the collapse that hurts everyone, including me. My restraint in seasons 3, 4, 5, and 6 was correct even when boat 1 was not restraining. I stayed at or below the sustainable share and limited the damage.

When I fall behind competitively mid-game and feel the urge to catch up, I resist. I caught 19.0 in season 2 when sustainable was 10.2 out of competitive desperation, and this single deviation set the pattern for stock collapse. The stock paid the price, and I paid it too. Catching up early does not catch up later—it prevents later.

When I reach the final season, I do not treat it as a free-for-all. By that point the stock is already depleted from my earlier aggression. Taking 3.3 on a stock of 29.8 in season 6 was correct, but it came too late to matter. I should have fished conservatively from the start, which would have left me with far more stock to harvest in the final seasons.

When I'm at any decision point, I ask: what total score do I end with if I stay cooperative throughout at the sustainable share? Then I ask: how much do I actually gain by deviating now? The answer in this episode was: I gained perhaps 10–12 fish by deviating in seasons 2, 3, and 4, but I lost roughly 20+ fish in seasons 5 and 6 due to stock collapse. Net loss of at least 10 points. I fish at the sustainable share every single season, without exception.

The moment I deviate from the sustainable share, I have lost. Stock collapse is not something that happens to me as a victim of others' greed—it is something I cause by my own hand. The only safe strategy is the only honest one. Hold the line from season 1 through season 6.
